why: Both texts treat direct or indirect fixing of fixed or minimum resale prices as a significant restriction by object, but A treats it as significant only 'grundsätzlich' (as a rule, so exceptions remain possible), while B states categorically that such agreements 'führen zu' a significant restriction, which changes the consequence that follows.

Both concern setting minimum or fixed resale prices, but A treats this as a significant restriction of competition under Art. 5(1) KG, while B makes it a presumed elimination of effective competition under Art. 5(4) KG, so a different consequence follows.

B carries A's rule that territorial and customer restrictions on resale are, by their object, a significant restriction of competition, but narrows what it covers by adding four exceptions (active-sale restrictions into reserved or exclusive territories, wholesaler sales to end users, sales to unauthorised dealers in selective distribution, and resale of supplied components to competing manufacturers).

B is still the rule against restricting the buyer's resale territory or customers, with the same four exceptions, but it changed in scope: it adds a carve-out for restrictions on the buyer's place of establishment, and it limits exception iii) to sales within the territory the supplier set for operating the selective distribution system.

B is recognisably A's hardcore territory/customer restriction rule. Its substance changed: it now applies only where the supplier runs neither an exclusive nor a selective distribution system, so A appears split across several provisions. Its exceptions were also altered, for example allowing active-sales restrictions passed on to direct customers, capping exclusive allocation at five distributors, and extending wholesale and spare-parts exceptions to passive sales.

B keeps A's rule on restricting sales to end users by dealers in selective distribution systems, but now covers only dealers operating at the retail level, and the opening drops 'grundsätzlich' ('as a rule'), so the conduct covered and the consequence both changed.

B still targets restrictions on active or passive sales to end users by retail-level members of a selective distribution system, but adds an exception allowing members to be barred from operating out of unauthorised establishments (and recasts the consequence as qualitatively severe rather than a significant restriction by object), so the rule covers less conduct.

B (iii) keeps A's rule that restricting retail-level selective distribution members' active or passive sales to end users is qualitatively severe, but it adds a new exception (c (i) 1.) permitting restrictions of active sales into territories or customer groups reserved to the supplier or exclusively allocated to up to five exclusive distributors, so it covers less conduct.

Both versions treat restrictions of cross-supplies between dealers within a selective distribution system, including dealers at different market levels, as a significant restriction of competition by object under Art. 5(1) KG; dropping 'zugelassenen' (members of a selective system are authorised dealers anyway) and 'grundsätzlich'/'namentlich' from the opening is rewording that does not change the conduct covered or its classification.

The restriction on the supplier selling spare parts to parties other than the participating dealer is the same conduct, but the opening changed from 'grundsätzlich als erhebliche Beeinträchtigung erachtet' (significant as a rule, allowing exceptions) to 'führen zu einer erheblichen Beeinträchtigung' (significant without qualification), so a stronger consequence now follows.

B keeps A's rule against restricting a supplier's sales of spare parts to end users and repairers, but narrows it to agreements between a parts supplier and a buyer who incorporates the parts, and exempts repairers or service providers the buyer has entrusted with repair or maintenance.

B carries A's rule on restricting a parts supplier from selling spare parts to end users, repairers or other service providers not entrusted by the buyer, but it adds wholesalers to the protected purchasers and so covers more conduct.

B keeps A's rule that non-compete obligations longer than five years are significant restrictions, but it drops the more-than-one-year post-termination limb, adds non-competes of indefinite duration, and adds an exception for buyers selling from the seller's premises, so the conduct covered has changed.

Both versions single out non-compete obligations of indefinite duration or longer than five years, with the same exception where the buyer sells from the seller's premises, as conduct significant by its object (2007) or qualitatively serious (2010); the change from 'Käufer' to 'Abnehmer' and the reworded sentence opening do not alter what is covered or what follows.

B keeps the rule that non-compete obligations of indefinite duration or longer than five years are qualitatively severe, but narrows the premises exception: rented premises now count only if rented from third parties not connected to the buyer, and the non-compete may not outlast the buyer's use of the premises, so more conduct is caught.

Both state the de minimis rule that other vertical agreements are normally not an appreciable restriction of competition below a market-share threshold, but B raises the threshold from 10% to 15%, applies it per participating undertaking rather than to shares held by all participants, and drops A's cumulative-network exception, so the rule covers different conduct.

Both versions apply the same 15% market-share safe harbour to vertical agreements outside the list of severe restrictions, and the change from 'Ziffer 10 (3) oder Ziffer 12' to 'Ziffer 12 (2) lit. a bis e' appears to only reflect the restructured numbering of that list, not a change in which agreements are excluded.

B keeps A's 15% market-share safe harbour for vertical agreements, but the excluded categories change from Ziffer 12(2) lit. a–e to Ziffer 10 or 12(2) lit. b–e, so the safe harbour now applies to a different set of agreements (unless this is purely a renumbering, which the text does not show).

B keeps A's 15 % market-share safe harbour, but the list of excluded agreements grows from Ziffer 12(2) lit. b–e (four categories) to Artikel 15 Buchstabe b–f (five categories), so the safe harbour now covers less conduct, though this assumes the extra letter f is a new category rather than a renumbering.

B keeps A's presumption for territorial allocation that excludes sales by out-of-territory distributors, but it now expressly exempts restrictions of passive sales falling under the exceptions in Article 15 letters b to d, so the rule covers less conduct.

Both require a case-by-case examination of whether a supplier's (Hersteller/Lieferant, now Anbieter) price recommendations to resellers or dealers are an unlawful agreement under Art. 5 KG; B only names the relevant paragraphs (Abs. 4 i.V.m. Abs. 1) more precisely, without changing the conduct covered or the consequence.

The lettered point names the same conduct: price recommendations given only to resellers or dealers rather than publicly, with only a spelling change from Weiterverkäufer to Wiederverkäufer; but its function changed, from a circumstance weighed in assessing a price recommendation to one that can prompt the authority to take a price recommendation up.

The circumstance is the same in both versions, that a significant share of resellers or dealers actually follow the price recommendations, but its consequence changed: in A it is a factor weighed when examining the recommendations, while in B it is only a reason the authority may take them up for scrutiny.

B is recognisably A's rule on post-contractual non-compete obligations, but its scope changed: A covered only non-competes lasting more than one year (exempt if conditions i–iii were met), while B covers all post-contractual non-competes and makes the one-year limit an extra condition (iv) for the exception.

B keeps A's rule that post-term non-competes are qualitatively severe, with the same four cumulative exceptions, and merges points i) and j) as separate rules; but B leaves out A's sentence that restrictions on using and disclosing non-public know-how may last indefinitely, so B carries only part of A.

The conduct is the same (targeted restrictions on multi-brand distribution of specific competing suppliers' brands in selective systems, with 'Lieferanten' merely reworded as 'Anbieter'), but the stated consequence changed from such agreements leading to a significant impairment of competition under Art. 5(1) KG by their object to their being regarded as qualitatively serious.

Both lower the market-share threshold to 5 % where parallel networks of vertical agreements with similar effects cumulatively restrict competition, and both treat a cumulative foreclosure effect as unlikely below 30 % market coverage; B's added sentence on suppliers or dealers at or below 5 % elaborates the same threshold without changing what the rule covers.

Both state that a vertical agreement significantly restricting competition must be checked for justification under Art. 5(2) KG and is unlawful absent efficiency grounds; specifying 'vertikale Wettbewerbsabrede' only makes explicit the scope the notice already had.

B keeps A's 30% market-share safe harbour but adds a second condition that the buyer's share on its purchasing market must also not exceed 30%, narrowing the covered conduct (and the exception reference changes from Ziffer 12 to Ziffer 12 (2)).

The 30% safe harbour is the same, but B also excludes agreements under Ziffer 10 and drops the condition that cumulative-effect agreements must significantly impair competition, so it covers less conduct.

Both state the 30% market-share safe harbour for supplier and buyer, excluding the hardcore restrictions and the qualitatively serious restrictions and agreements with cumulative market effects; only the gendered forms and the numbering of the cross-references (Ziffern 10 and 12(2) become Articles 12 and 15 VertBek) changed.

B states the same rule as A (agreements significantly restricting competition not covered by paragraph 2 are assessed case by case and are justified where they increase economic efficiency under Art. 5(2) KG and the restriction is necessary), differing only in wording ('vertikale Wettbewerbsabreden', 'Absatz 2' instead of 'Ziffer 16 (2)') and numbering.
B restates A's free-rider justification for avoiding inefficiently low sales promotion verbatim except for gendered forms and renumbering, so the conduct and consequence are unchanged.
B states the identical justification ground (avoiding double marginalisation when both manufacturer and distributor have market power), differing only in gendered forms and paragraph numbering.

A combines the micro-enterprise rule from Ziffer 9(2) with the definition of purely qualitative selective distribution, and B carries only the definition, unchanged in substance, so B holds just part of A.

Both define purely qualitative selective distribution as dealer selection based solely on objective qualitative criteria tied to the product's requirements; B drops only A's illustrative 'z.B.' examples and uses the gendered form 'Händlerinnen', which changes neither the conduct covered nor its consequence.

B keeps A's statement of the Art. 5 Abs. 4 KG presumption for resale price maintenance and passive-sales bans, but drops A's sentence that resale price maintenance disguised as price recommendations also falls under it, so B carries only part of A's rule.

B restates A's description of the presumption under Article 5(4) KG for minimum or fixed resale prices and for passive-sales bans to dealers or end customers, differing only in added terminology ("vertikale Preisabreden"), wording and gendered forms.

Both concern how the Art. 5(4) KG presumption on vertical agreements is rebutted, but A excludes rebuttal by mere proof of interbrand competition, whereas B bases rebuttal on an overall market assessment of intrabrand and interbrand competition, which changes the rebuttal standard.

Both state that the provision specifies agreements presumed under Art. 5(4) KG to eliminate effective competition and that rebuttal of the presumption rests on an overall market assessment (intrabrand and interbrand competition), differing only in numbering (Ziffer 10/11 vs. Artikel 12/13 VertBek) and minor wording.
B keeps A's 15% market-share and no-cumulative-effect de minimis rule but narrows it by excluding vertical agreements under Ziffer 10 or 12(2) lit. b to e, so it covers less conduct.

B carries A's de-minimis rule (15 % threshold, no cumulative effect) but changes its substance: under cumulative effect, case-by-case assessment now applies only if a 5 % market-share threshold is also exceeded, and the excluded hardcore restrictions extend to letters b to f instead of b to e.

B keeps A's rule that a significantly restrictive agreement must be justified on efficiency grounds and is otherwise unlawful, but it drops A's statement that no efficiency grounds can be invoked where effective competition is eliminated and adds that such agreements remain subject to sanctions under Art. 49a KG even when the presumption is rebutted.

B only specifies 'Abreden' as 'vertikale Wettbewerbsabreden', which Article 5(4) KG already covers. The rule is unchanged: agreements that indirectly lead to minimum or fixed prices or absolute territorial protection fall under that provision.

B only specifies 'Abreden' as 'vertikale Wettbewerbsabreden', which the notice on vertical agreements already covered, so the conduct (recommendation-style agreements fixing minimum/fixed prices or absolute territorial protection) and its consequence under Art. 5(4) KG are unchanged.

B keeps A's case-by-case weighing of qualitative and quantitative criteria but limits it to 'all other' vertical agreements, carving out the agreements dealt with separately in point (a), so the rule now covers less conduct.

B keeps A's rule that all other vertical agreements are assessed case by case on both qualitative and quantitative criteria, with either a qualitatively severe or a quantitatively substantial agreement able to be significant; only the wording changed ('Beeinträchtigung' to 'Wettbewerbsabrede', an added cross-reference to Art. 15, 'Umgekehrt' to 'Ebenso').

B covers the same conduct as A, the restriction of the buyer's ability to set its own resale price with the same carve-out for maximum and recommended prices, but the consequence changes from being treated as qualitatively severe to a presumption that effective competition is eliminated under Article 5(4) KG.

B keeps A's presumption for fixing minimum or fixed resale prices but drops the clause allowing maximum prices and price recommendations unless pressure or incentives make them act as fixed or minimum prices, so B carries only part of A's rule.

Both cover recommended prices that act as fixed or minimum resale prices because of pressure or incentives, but the consequence changed: in A they are qualitatively severe, and in B they are in principle significant restrictions of competition.

A has vertical agreements whose presumption is rebutted assessed for significance case by case on qualitative and quantitative criteria, whereas B treats Article 5(4) agreements as significant in principle once the presumption is rebutted and keeps the weighing only for other vertical agreements, so a different consequence now follows for A's conduct.

B restates A's explanation (Art. 5(4) agreements generally meet the significance criterion if the presumption is rebutted, all others are assessed case by case on qualitative and quantitative criteria, and qualitatively severe agreements face lower quantitative requirements) with only renumbering (Ziffer 12 to Art. 14/15 VertBek) and wording changes such as 'Wettbewerbsbeeinträchtigung' for 'Wettbewerbsbeschränkung'.

Both state that vertical agreements under Art. 5(4) KG in principle meet the significance criterion of Art. 5(1) KG if the presumption is rebutted; only the cross-reference and the explicit 'vertikale Wettbewerbsabreden' wording changed.

Both state that certain agreements in selective distribution systems are qualified as qualitatively severe while their significance (Art. 5(1) KG) and justification (Art. 5(2) KG) must be examined case by case; only the numbering of the cited provisions and minor wording changed.

B states the same rule that restrictions on sales by selective distribution members to unauthorised dealers within the supplier's designated territory, including limiting warranty to products bought from authorised dealers, are not qualitatively severe, differing only in gendered forms, article references and 'Wettbewerbsabrede' wording.

B restates A's rule that restrictions of active or passive sales by authorised retailers to end users and between authorised dealers are qualitatively severe, and that excluding passive sales by foreign partners amounts to absolute territorial protection under Art. 5(4) KG, differing only in gendered forms, article numbering and cross-references.

Both concern combining exclusive and selective distribution in the same territory, but A treats it as severe only when active sales are restricted, while B treats the combination itself as severe without that condition, including the wholesale/retail case.

The 15 %, 5 % and 50 % rule for selective distribution is unchanged, but the restrictions that rule out the safe harbour now point to 'Art. 12 oder Art. 15 lit. c' instead of 'Ziff. 10 oder Ziff. 12 Abs. 2 lit. b bis e'; this looks like a narrowing from four lettered restrictions to one, so it is treated as a change in which conduct is covered, though it may only be renumbering and should be checked against both versions of the VertBek.

B repeats A's rule that selective distribution systems meeting the three cumulative conditions of the notice are admissible regardless of market shares for lack of a significant restriction of competition, changing only the cross-reference from Ziff. 14 to Artikel 17 VertBek.

B keeps A's rule that online-sales restrictions accompanied by qualifying circumstances can fall under Art. 5(4) KG after a case-by-case assessment, but it drops the vertical price agreement as a possible classification and widens the subject from bans or restrictions of internet sales to vertical agreements concerning online trade in general.

A lists circumstances that qualify conduct as a vertical price agreement, mainly supplier pressure such as influencing discounts, threats, delays or termination, whereas B describes direct contractual means of fixing resale prices and compliance with a requested price increase, which is other conduct even though both concern vertical price agreements.

B keeps A's examples of hardcore absolute territorial protection (blocking website access, redirecting customers, ending transactions by card address), but broadens them from Swiss customers and automatic redirects to customers from any other territory and redirects generally, and adds an exception that an obligation to set links to the supplier's or other sellers' online shops is not a qualifying circumstance.

Both treat restrictions of the buyer's internet sales as qualitatively severe, but B changes the scope: it now covers only restrictions that prevent effective use of the internet, and it extends to the buyer's customers, entire online advertising channels and own online shops, without A's passive-sales justification.

Both govern online-sales criteria imposed on authorised dealers in selective distribution, but A treats criteria not equivalent to brick-and-mortar criteria as a qualitatively severe agreement, while B drops the equivalence requirement and treats such criteria as severe only if they indirectly aim to prevent effective use of the internet.

B keeps A's rule that the significance and efficiency justification of internet-sales restrictions are assessed case by case, but changes what it covers: it is now limited to restrictions preventing effective use of the internet for online sales, and it adds restrictions on using whole online advertising channels.

B restates A's rule on sanctioning vertical agreements that eliminate or significantly restrict competition without efficiency justification, including the presumption for minimum/fixed prices and absolute territorial protection, with only terminological changes ("Wettbewerbsabrede") and updated cross-references to the notice's numbering.

B keeps A's definition of a vertical price agreement as a conscious and intended cooperation on minimum or fixed prices, but drops A's statements that price recommendations can be a concerted practice and that price agreements disguised as recommendations fall under Art. 5 Abs. 4 KG, so B carries only part of A's rule.

B keeps A's rule that resale prices can be fixed indirectly and its examples (conditional rebates and advertising refunds, maximum discounts, threats and supply delays), but it expressly adds conduct A did not list, namely fixing the resale margin, minimum advertised prices and tying resale prices to competitors' prices, so it covers more conduct.

B keeps A's three-element test for absolute territorial protection, but it adds that under exclusive distribution assigning Switzerland alone suffices, drops internet sales from the listed forms of passive sales, and extends passive sales to private calls for expressions of interest, which changes what the rule covers.

B drops A's requirement that Swiss distribution partners are also assigned the territory of Switzerland, so the example now covers any EEA territory assignment combined with an export ban, while the gendered forms and the 'offen bzw. frei' wording are only editorial.

B states the same rule that absolute territorial protection can be imposed indirectly through any measure that discourages dealers from serving requests from certain territories, including unpaid warranty services and purchasing restrictions; the changes are rewording, renumbering, gendered forms and a slightly longer list of illustrative examples under the unchanged catch-all 'sämtliche Massnahmen'.

B keeps A's list of situations that do not meet the presumption of Art. 5 Abs. 4 KG, but its substance changed: the intra-group exemption no longer requires that there be no foreclosure of dealers outside the group, the passive-sales obligation now names manufacturers rather than suppliers, and the customer-group bullet drops both the classification as qualitatively severe and the internet-sales statement.

B keeps the presumption for fixing minimum or fixed prices and only spells out what that means: maximum prices and price recommendations stay outside unless they in fact work as fixed or minimum prices, so the conduct covered and the consequence are unchanged.

A presumes that fixing minimum or fixed prices eliminates effective competition, while B lists securing the uniformity and quality of contract products as a ground companies may invoke for efficiency justification under Art. 5(2) KG, which is other conduct and another rule.

A presumes elimination of effective competition for agreements fixing minimum or fixed prices, whereas B lists a circumstance (price level clearly higher than in neighbouring countries) that may prompt scrutiny of price recommendations, which is other conduct and another rule.
A treats restrictions of cross-supplies within a selective distribution system as qualitatively severe, while B only defines what a cross-supply is and attaches no consequence to restricting it.

B merges several selective-distribution rules, but its point (ii) still treats restrictions of cross-supplies between members of a selective distribution system, whether at the same or different trade levels, as qualitatively severe, which is A's rule unchanged.

A classifies restrictions of cross-supplies between distributors within a selective distribution system as qualitatively severe, whereas B merely defines what a selective distribution system is and states no rule on cross-supply restrictions or their consequence.

B's exception i) carries A's rule on restricting resales into territories or customer groups the supplier reserves for itself, as long as passive sales stay free, but it changes it: A treats such restrictions as possibly justified under Art. 5(2) KG, while B excludes them from by-object significant restrictions and extends the exception to territories allocated exclusively to another dealer.

A sets out when restrictions on the dealer's resale territory or customer group reserved to the supplier can be justified under Article 5(2) KG, provided passive sales and customers' resales remain free. B only defines active approach of customers in a territory or customer group reserved to the supplier or allocated exclusively to another dealer, which is another rule even though it uses the same terms.

A sets out an efficiency justification under Art. 5(2) KG for restricting a dealer's resale territory or customers to those the supplier reserves for itself, provided the dealer may still fill unsolicited orders and its customers' resales are not limited; B only lists conduct (filling unsolicited orders from a territory, cross-supplies within a selective distribution system) without stating that justification rule.

A is a justification rule allowing resale restrictions on territories or customer groups assigned exclusively to another dealer, on condition that passive sales and customers' resales stay free; B (partly garbled) only lists conduct that must remain possible, namely filling unsolicited orders from a territory and cross-supplies within a selective distribution system, and does not carry A's justification rule.

Both concern restricting a dealer's resale into territories or customer groups exclusively allocated to another dealer while passive sales stay free, but B changes the substance: such restrictions are no longer a ground for justification under Art. 5(2) KG and instead fall outside the by-object significant restriction, and B also covers areas the supplier reserves to itself and drops A's condition that the dealer's customers' resales must not be restricted.

A is a justification rule under Art. 5(2) KG that lets restrictions on resale into territories or customer groups exclusively allocated to another dealer be justified, on conditions; B only defines active sales into territories or customer groups reserved to the supplier or to another dealer, and states no permission or consequence.

A says that restricting wholesalers from selling directly to end consumers can be justified on efficiency grounds, whereas B says that restricting active or passive sales to end consumers by retail-level dealers in selective distribution systems is a significant restriction by object, so the conduct and the rule both differ.

Both concern restrictions on wholesalers selling directly to end consumers, but A treats them as possibly justified on efficiency grounds under Art. 5(2) KG after a significant restriction is found, whereas B excludes them from the by-object significant restrictions under Art. 5(1) KG, so a different consequence follows for the same conduct.

A says restrictions that stop wholesalers from selling directly to end consumers may be justified for efficiency, whereas B defines active approaches to individual customers in a territory or customer group reserved to the supplier or allocated exclusively to another distributor.

A says a restriction can be justified when it stops an authorised dealer in a selective distribution system from reselling to non-authorised dealers, whereas B treats restrictions on active or passive sales to end users by retail-level dealers in such systems as a significant restriction by object, which is other conduct with another consequence.

A covers restrictions that stop an authorised dealer in a selective distribution system from reselling to non-authorised dealers and treats them as potentially justified for efficiency, while B covers restrictions on cross-supplies between dealers within the system and treats them as significant restrictions by object, so the conduct and the rule differ.

A concerns the possible justification of restrictions preventing an authorised dealer in a selective distribution system from reselling to unauthorised dealers, whereas B treats as a significant restriction by object the restriction of multi-brand distribution targeting specific competing suppliers' brands, which is other conduct with another consequence.

Both concern restricting the dealer from reselling supplier-provided components to third parties who would use them to make competing products. In A (2002), such a restriction is a possible efficiency justification under Art. 5(2) KG, examined only once a significant restriction has been found. In B (2007, point iv), it is an exception that means the restriction is not a significant restriction by object under Art. 5(1) KG at all, so the consequence differs.

A concerns a possible justification for restricting the dealer from reselling components supplied for incorporation to third parties making competing products, whereas B classifies as a significant restriction by object any restriction preventing the supplier from selling components or spare parts to parties other than the dealers in the agreement, so the conduct and the consequence both differ.

A justifies restrictions on a dealer's resale of components supplied for incorporation to third parties making competing products, whereas B defines selective distribution agreements (sale only to authorised dealers and a ban on resale to unauthorised dealers), which is other conduct.

Both state the de minimis rule that vertical agreements outside the listed hardcore restrictions are not significant below a market-share threshold, but B is an operative safe harbour with a fixed 15% threshold, A's cumulative-effect condition is not in it, and A's 'only then' framing and Article 7 caveat are gone, so the scope has changed.

B carries only A's last sentence, that the notice says nothing about assessment under Art. 7 KG, and extends it to horizontal agreements under Art. 5(3) KG, while A's main rule on when other vertical agreements count as insignificant is not in B, so under the split rule this is a partial carry-over.

B keeps A's core rule that an agreement is in principle insignificant only if it stays below the market-share threshold and has no cumulative effect, but the threshold is now stated as 15% (the 2002 notice's Ziffer 4 threshold was 10%), and B leaves out A's other statements: that the list of significant agreements does not make other agreements insignificant, and that the notice says nothing about Article 7 KG.

B carries only the part of A that treats recommendation-form agreements on minimum or fixed prices as covered by Art. 5(4) KG, and it changes that rule by requiring that such recommendations rest on an agreement or concerted practice and by extending it to their object or effect; the core price-fixing presumption sits elsewhere, so A was split.

Both concern resale price maintenance through fixed or minimum prices, but B attaches a different consequence (qualitatively severe rather than a presumed elimination of competition) and narrows the coverage of recommendations to those that actually act as fixed or minimum prices because of pressure or incentives.

A presumes that agreements fixing minimum or fixed resale prices, including those disguised as recommendations, eliminate competition, whereas B is a separate rule that price recommendations by suppliers must be examined case by case for unlawfulness.

Both govern how the presumption that effective competition is eliminated can be rebutted, but A says proof of interbrand competition alone cannot rebut it, while B makes an overall market assessment decisive and lets sufficient interbrand competition alone rebut it.

B is a recital that summarises the notice's provisions on rebutting the presumption, whereas A is an operative provision, and the protocol treats a recital and an operative provision as different; B also looks at overall market competition rather than barring rebuttal by interbrand competition alone.

A says the presumption of eliminating competition cannot be rebutted merely by showing interbrand competition, whereas B is a recital about what follows once the presumption is rebutted (efficiency justification and sanctions), so it states another rule and is a recital rather than an operative provision.

A says the agreements listed in Ziffer 10(1) remain a significant restriction of competition even after the presumption is rebutted, whereas B, a recital, only sets out the next steps (efficiency justification under Art. 5(2) KG and sanctions under Art. 49a KG) and treats significance as a condition to be checked rather than stating it follows.

A is an operative rule that the listed agreements remain a significant restriction of competition even when the presumption is rebutted, whereas B is a recital summarising which agreements fall under the presumption and how it is rebutted, not that consequence.

A is an operative provision (Ziffer 10(3)) treating the listed agreements as significant even after the presumption is rebutted, while B is a recital (IX) of the next version that summarises the operative provisions on case-by-case assessment of significance, and the protocol classes a recital and an operative provision as different.

A concerns case-by-case assessment of price recommendations under Art. 5(4) with 5(1) KG, whereas B states the general efficiency-justification test under Art. 5(2) KG for any significantly restrictive vertical agreement, which is other conduct and another rule.

Both concern recommendations under Art. 5(4) KG, but A requires a case-by-case check of price recommendations, whereas B states that recommendation-form vertical agreements fixing minimum or fixed prices fall under Art. 5(4) and extends this to absolute territorial protection, changing both the scope and the consequence.

A specifically requires case-by-case examination of suppliers' price recommendations to resellers for an unlawful agreement under Art. 5(4) with 5(1) KG, whereas B is a general rule subjecting vertical agreements that significantly restrict competition and are not covered by paragraph 2 to case-by-case assessment and sets out the economic-efficiency justification, so it concerns other conduct and states another rule.

A is about price recommendations given in a non-publicly accessible way only to resellers being a circumstance that may prompt scrutiny, whereas B states the presumption of elimination of effective competition for agreements fixing minimum or fixed resale prices, which is other conduct and another rule.

A concerns price recommendations given only to resellers as a circumstance prompting scrutiny, whereas B concerns a qualitatively severe restriction on a parts supplier's ability to sell spare parts to end users and independent repairers, which is entirely other conduct.

A names non-public communication of price recommendations only to resellers as a circumstance that can prompt scrutiny of price recommendations, whereas B lists avoiding free-rider-induced underinvestment in sales promotion as an efficiency justification under Art. 5(2) KG, which is other conduct and another rule.

Both concern price recommendations combined with pressure or incentives, but A treats this as one circumstance weighed in the assessment, whereas B makes it part of a test under which recommendations count as qualitatively severe only if, through that pressure or those incentives, they actually operate as fixed or minimum resale prices.

A concerns price recommendations combined with pressure or specific incentives, whereas B concerns a price level markedly higher than in neighbouring countries, which is other conduct even though both list circumstances relevant to price recommendations.

B keeps A's rule that price recommendations combined with pressure or incentives are problematic, but changes the consequence: in A this was one factor in a case-by-case assessment, while in B recommendations that, through pressure or incentives, actually work as fixed or minimum resale prices count as qualitatively severe restrictions.

A concerns price recommendations in Swiss francs that are not expressly marked as non-binding being a reason for scrutiny, whereas B is a recital about aligning the notice with case law and EU rules, which is other content altogether.

A names a specific circumstance (price recommendations printed in CHF on products, packaging or catalogues without being expressly marked non-binding) that may prompt scrutiny of price recommendations, whereas B states that Article 5(4) KG covers vertical agreements disguised as recommendations that aim at or result in minimum or fixed prices or absolute territorial protection, which is a different rule about other conduct.

A concerns price recommendations not expressly marked as non-binding as a circumstance prompting scrutiny, whereas B concerns restrictions on a parts supplier's ability to sell spare parts to independent repairers and end users as a qualitatively severe vertical restraint, which is other conduct and another rule.

A names a price level markedly higher than in neighbouring countries as a circumstance that can prompt scrutiny of price recommendations, whereas B states the presumption that effective competition is eliminated by fixing minimum or fixed resale prices, which is other conduct and another rule.

A names a higher price level than in neighbouring countries as a circumstance prompting scrutiny of price recommendations, whereas B lists avoidance of double marginalisation as an efficiency justification undertakings may invoke under Art. 5(2) KG, which is other conduct and another rule.

A names a higher price level than in neighbouring countries as a circumstance that can prompt scrutiny of price recommendations, whereas B states that Art. 5(4) KG also covers recommendation-style vertical agreements aimed at minimum or fixed prices or absolute territorial protection, which is another rule.

A lists actual compliance with price recommendations by a significant share of resellers as a circumstance prompting scrutiny, whereas B lists achieving economies of scale in distribution as an efficiency justification under Article 5(2) KG, which is other conduct and another rule.

A names a circumstance (price recommendations actually followed by a significant share of resellers) that may prompt scrutiny of price recommendations, whereas B states the presumption that vertical agreements fixing minimum or fixed resale prices eliminate effective competition, which is other conduct and another rule.

A names, as a circumstance that may prompt scrutiny of price recommendations, that a significant share of resellers actually follow them, whereas B lists avoiding inefficiently low sales-promotion efforts caused by free-riding as an efficiency justification under Art. 5(2) KG, which is other conduct and another rule.

A treats targeted restrictions on multi-brand distribution in selective distribution systems as qualitatively severe, whereas B merely defines what a selective distribution system is, sharing only the topic and not the rule.

A treats as qualitatively severe the targeted restriction of multi-brand distribution against specific competing brands in selective distribution, whereas B concerns territorial/customer resale restrictions, cross-supply restrictions and end-user sales restrictions within selective distribution, which is other conduct.

A treats restrictions on multi-brand distribution in selective systems targeting specific competitors' brands as qualitatively severe, whereas B merely defines purely qualitative selective distribution, which is other conduct and states another rule.

A requires a case-by-case check of whether the restriction of competition is significant (Erheblichkeit), while B starts from agreements already found to restrict competition significantly and subjects them to a case-by-case check of efficiency justification under Art. 5(2) KG.

A requires case-by-case review of whether the restriction of competition is significant for all other agreements, for the Ziffer 12 exceptions and for non-compliant selective distribution, whereas B creates a 30 % market-share safe harbour under which agreements are generally treated as justified without case-by-case review, so B is about justification rather than significance.

A states that all other agreements and the exceptions of point 12 (notably selective distribution not meeting point 8(4)) must be assessed case by case for significance, whereas B states that purely qualitative selective distribution meeting three cumulative conditions does not significantly restrict competition, which is another rule about other conduct.

Both explain how a listed category of severe vertical agreements is assessed for significance, but B no longer treats them as significant regardless of market share; it requires a case-by-case overall assessment in which only lower quantitative requirements apply, so the consequence changed.

A is an explanatory note summarising which agreements must have the significance of their restriction examined case by case, whereas B is an operative provision subjecting agreements already found significantly restrictive to case-by-case examination of efficiency justification, so both the kind of text and the rule differ.

A covers both hard-core restrictions (significant regardless of market share) and case-by-case review of all other agreements except those under Ziffer 13; B keeps only the case-by-case part, now framed around the 15% de minimis threshold and cumulative effects, so it carries only part of A's rule.

A is a Roman-numeral recital of the 2017 notice that summarises the efficiency test, while B is the operative provision 18(1), and the protocol treats a summarising recital and an operative provision as different even when they say the same thing.

A is a recital that summarises the efficiency-justification test for hard-core vertical agreements once the presumption of eliminated competition is rebutted, while B is an operative provision setting out the case-by-case review and efficiency justification for agreements not covered by paragraph 2, and the protocol treats a recital and an operative provision as different.

B merges A's rule with other rules (de minimis in X, non-binding effect in XII) but its section XI restates A's rule without substantive change: the efficiency justification test after rebuttal of the presumption, the agreement is unlawful absent efficiency grounds, and it remains subject to sanctions under Art. 49a KG; only the reference number (Ziffer 16 to Artikel 18) and the wording differ.

B still covers recommendations that in effect operate as fixed or minimum resale prices, but its substance changed: it places them under the Article 5(4) KG presumption, requires an agreement or concerted practice instead of pressure or incentives, includes recommendations that merely aim at such prices, and extends the rule to absolute territorial protection.

A is about price recommendations that act like fixed or minimum prices because of pressure or incentives and are treated as significant restrictions, whereas B is the hardcore presumption for directly fixing minimum or fixed resale prices, which corresponds to the old Ziffer 10(1) lit. a that A only cross-references.

A treats price recommendations that, through pressure or incentives, actually work like fixed or minimum resale prices as significant restrictions of competition, whereas B defines what vertical agreements are and says nothing about price recommendations.

B carries A's rule that restricting authorised dealers' sales to end users and between authorised dealers in selective distribution is qualitatively severe, but it is no longer limited to internet-sales bans and now extends to active as well as passive sales.

A treats bans or restrictions on internet sales in selective distribution as severe because they restrict passive sales, whereas B states that restricting members' sales to unauthorised dealers within the system's territory is not severe, which concerns other conduct and states another rule.

Both treat internet-sales restrictions as qualitatively severe, but B changes the rule's reach. A covered any ban or restriction within selective distribution systems, grounded in the passive-sales rules. B applies generally to restrictions that prevent effective use of the internet, including de facto bans, blocking whole online advertising channels and preventing an own online shop.

B keeps A's rule that online-sales quality requirements and marketplace bans are not qualitatively severe, but extends the marketplace point beyond luxury selective distribution to any distribution system, adds the condition that the restriction must not indirectly aim to prevent effective use of the internet, and drops the example of requiring a physical shop.

A concerns quality requirements a supplier may impose on dealers' internet sales (physical shop requirement, ban on third-party platforms for luxury goods), whereas B concerns restrictions on selective-distribution members selling to unauthorised dealers within the supplier's designated territory, which is other conduct despite the shared 'not qualitatively severe' framing.

B keeps A's rule that online-sales quality requirements, including a physical-shop requirement and a marketplace ban, are not qualitatively severe, but it widens it: the marketplace ban is no longer limited to luxury goods in selective distribution, and new examples such as an absolute minimum offline sales volume are added.
